questions.q: Why does testing 100 random, meaningless trading rules against the same 5-year dataset tend to produce at least one rule with an impressive Sharpe ratio?
options: Because all trading rules are secretly profitable
Because with enough independent tries, pure chance guarantees some will appear to fit that specific sample's noise well, even with zero real predictive power
Because 5 years of data is too short to test any rule
Because random rules always outperform designed strategies
questions.explain: This is the data snooping / multiple-testing problem: a finite historical sample contains limited real signal but a large amount of noise, and testing enough variations makes finding one that fits the noise well nearly certain.

questions.q: In the parameter sweep example testing ~3,000 (fast_n, slow_n) combinations and keeping the single best Sharpe ratio, why is that reported best_sharpe considered an inflated, unreliable estimate?
options: Because the code has a syntax error
Because it is the maximum of thousands of noisy samples evaluated on the same data used to search, not a single honest, pre-specified test
Because moving average strategies never work
Because Sharpe ratios cannot be computed for parameter sweeps
questions.explain: Selecting the best result out of many trials on the same dataset is a fundamentally different (and much more optimistic) statistical quantity than evaluating one pre-specified strategy a single time.

questions.q: Why does purging remove a training observation whose label window overlaps the test fold, even when the fold boundary itself looks clean?
options: Because a label spanning multiple future bars (e.g., a 5-day forward return) can reach into the test period, leaking test-period information into training even though the index boundary looks fine
Purging is unnecessary if walk-forward analysis is already being used
Purging only matters for labels that span exactly one bar
Purging removes test-set observations, not training observations
questions.explain: The subtle leak purging fixes is specifically about label windows reaching across the fold boundary -- a leak walk-forward's ordering alone doesn't catch, since the index split itself looks clean.

questions.q: In the hands-on leaky-strategy exercise, what was the actual bug causing a Sharpe ratio of 20.485 on data with zero real signal?
options: The strategy used today's own realized return to decide today's position -- effectively trading with knowledge of the outcome before placing the trade
The strategy used too large a position size
The random number generator was seeded incorrectly
The strategy traded too infrequently to generate a real signal
questions.explain: Using daily_returns[i] to decide positions[i], when positions[i] is then multiplied by that same daily_returns[i], is same-bar leakage -- the strategy already knows the answer before 'predicting' it.

questions.q: What is walk-forward analysis, and why is it considered a more realistic defense against overfitting than a single static train/test split?
options: It tests the strategy only once on the full dataset

It repeatedly re-fits parameters on a rolling window of past data and tests on the immediately following period, rolling forward through time — simulating how a researcher would actually have to operate using only data available at each point
It removes the need for any out-of-sample testing
It only works for strategies with zero parameters
questions.explain: Walk-forward analysis mimics the real constraint that a live researcher only has access to data up to 'now' at each point, re-optimizing periodically rather than relying on one fixed split — giving a more honest, if still imperfect, performance estimate.
